h1: The 6 Best Countertop Microwaves of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six countertop microwaves compared on capacity, wattage, sensor cooking and price to help you pick the right size.
summary: The TOSHIBA at 1.2 cu ft and 1000W is the best countertop microwave for most kitchens, balancing size, power and price. The Sharp SMC2266KS has the roomiest interior with 1200W. The Panasonic NN-SN686S adds speed in a mid-size body, the Farberware brings sensor cooking, the COMFEE' serves dorms, and the NN-SN76LS is the inverter option.
intro: Most microwave shoppers compare cubic feet and move on, then wonder why the biggest box heats a bowl of soup slowly. Interior volume says how much fits; wattage says how hard the magnetron works on what is inside. Pair a large cavity with a weak rating and you get a spacious oven that stirs lukewarm leftovers, while a smaller, stronger unit often feels faster in daily use.

So this ranking reads both numbers together. Eight microwaves were considered and six kept, each a distinct model, judged on the spec sheet: capacity, wattage, cooking features, footprint and price bucket. Listings with unreliable or unclear numbers were dropped. One inverter model survives despite a missing wattage figure, and the ranking marks that gap against it.

products.name: TOSHIBA Countertop Microwave Oven
products.verdict: A 1.2 cu ft, 1000W microwave that suits most kitchens.
products.description:
The TOSHIBA is the safe center of this category. It lists 1.2 cu ft of capacity and 1000W, in the $100 to $200 bucket. That interior takes a standard dinner plate and a mug without crowding the counter, and 1000W is a strong enough rating that popcorn, soup and frozen dinners finish in sensible times.

It ranks first since 1000W comfortably beats the COMFEE' at 700W and costs less than the Panasonic and Sharp. The price of that balance is giving up the Sharp's larger interior and the Panasonic's 1200W.

It fits couples and small families who want one appliance that does everything adequately. The caveat is the listing itself: few extra features are named, so there is no sensor cooking to speak of, and a big family should step up to the Sharp.
products.idealFor: Couples and small families wanting a balanced size.
products.skipIf: You need to fit large platters.

products.name: Sharp SMC2266KS 2.2 cu. ft. 1200W Stainless Steel Countertop
products.verdict: The biggest cavity here with 1200W behind it.
products.description:
The Sharp SMC2266KS answers the question of space. Its 2.2 cu ft interior in stainless steel comes with 1200W, in the $200 to $500 bucket, which is enough room for a casserole dish or a large platter that would not turn in the others. Higher wattage means the extra volume still heats at a decent pace.

It ranks second because it costs more than the TOSHIBA, but offers more than three times the interior of the COMFEE' and more watts than any other pick here. For a family cooking big dishes, that math is hard to argue with.

Buy it for large plates and batch reheating. The caveat is the footprint. A cavity this size needs real counter, so measure width, depth and the clearance above before ordering, and skip it if your counter is tight.

products.name: Panasonic Microwave Oven NN-SN686S Stainless Steel
products.verdict: 1200W in a 1.2 cu ft stainless body.
products.description:
The Panasonic NN-SN686S puts 1200W into a 1.2 cu ft stainless steel body, in the $200 to $500 bucket. The same capacity as the TOSHIBA but 200W more means shorter heating times, which you notice most on dense foods and reheated plates.

It ranks third because the extra power lands in a higher price bucket than the TOSHIBA, and for the same money the Sharp offers a much larger interior. You are choosing speed over space or savings.

Buy it if you want a quick, compact unit and a stainless finish that matches other appliances. The caveat is price versus the TOSHIBA: unless 1200W is important to your routine, 1000W is enough, and the saved money covers a good deal else in the kitchen.
products.idealFor: Buyers wanting speed in a mid-size unit.

products.name: Farberware 1.6 Cu. Ft. Countertop Microwave Oven
products.verdict: Smart sensor auto cook and defrost at 1100W.
products.description:
The Farberware is the only pick that lists Smart Sensor Auto Cook. It offers 1.6 cu ft, 1100 watts and a defrost setting, in the $100 to $200 bucket. Sensor cooking reads steam released by food and adjusts time, so reheating a plate stops before the edges dry out.

It takes fourth place since it sits between the TOSHIBA and the Sharp on capacity and watts, and gives up some power to the Sharp. The sensor features are the main reason to choose it, and they cost less than the Panasonic.

Buy it if you reheat and defrost often. The caveat is pedigree: the brand has a thinner reputation than Panasonic or Sharp, and the listing says little beyond the feature list, so check the control layout and return terms.
products.idealFor: Cooks who reheat and defrost often.

products.name: COMFEE' Countertop Microwave Oven
products.verdict: A 0.7 cu ft, 700W unit with an ECO mode, for small spaces.
products.description:
The COMFEE' is the compact budget unit. It lists 0.7 cu ft, 700W and an ECO mode, in the $50 to $100 bucket, making it the cheapest and smallest here. A 0.7 cu ft cavity fits a bowl or mug and slides into a dorm or an office kitchen.

It ranks fifth because its capacity and wattage are the lowest in the list. Next to the TOSHIBA you give up 300W and half a cubic foot to save money, and every dish takes longer.

Buy it when counter space is the constraint and you mostly reheat drinks and small meals. The caveat is speed: a 700W rating heats more slowly, and a full dinner plate may not turn freely. Anyone cooking for a family should step up to the TOSHIBA or beyond.

products.name: Panasonic NN-SN76LS 1.6 cu.ft Cyclonic Inverter Countertop Microwave
products.verdict: A 1.6 cu ft inverter model with listed dimensions.
products.description:
The Panasonic NN-SN76LS is the inverter model. It is a Cyclonic Inverter oven with 1.6 cu ft of interior, in the $200 to $500 bucket, and the listing gives exact dimensions of 19.44 inches deep, 21.88 inches wide and 11.94 inches high. Inverter designs aim to deliver power more steadily rather than cycling it on and off, which can help with delicate foods.

It ranks last because the listing gives no wattage and the price bucket is higher than the Farberware, which has the same 1.6 cu ft capacity and does list its power.

Buy it if you measure your counter carefully and like the inverter approach. The caveat is the missing wattage, so confirm the power rating on the manufacturer page before you buy, since you cannot judge speed from this listing alone.

whatMatters.detail: Wattage is how much power the magnetron delivers, and it sets how fast food heats. A 700W unit takes noticeably longer than a 1200W unit on the same plate. Check the number in the title or bullets rather than assuming it from the brand, and be wary of listings that omit it, as the Panasonic NN-SN76LS does.

Cubic feet measures interior volume. A 0.7 cu ft unit may not hold a full dinner plate, while 2.2 cu ft fits large dishes. Compare capacity with the plate or casserole you use most, and check the turntable diameter if it is given, since volume alone does not tell you whether a plate rotates cleanly without catching the wall.

Sensor cooking adjusts time based on steam, so you do not guess for reheating. The Farberware lists Smart Sensor Auto Cook, and it matters most if you warm plated leftovers or frozen meals. Look for the words sensor or auto cook in the features list, and distinguish them from simple preset buttons, which only run a fixed time.

A bigger interior means a bigger body. Measure counter space and cabinet clearance above and beside the unit, including room for the door to open. Look for exterior dimensions on the listing, as the Panasonic NN-SN76LS provides, and compare them with your space rather than trusting the capacity number, because cabinets and walls limit real placement.

Stainless steel looks sharp and matches many appliances, though it shows fingerprints. The Sharp SMC2266KS and Panasonic NN-SN686S both use it. Check the finish in the title, since the same microwave often comes in black or white, and the model suffix tells you which finish you are buying, so read it carefully.

faq.q: What size countertop microwave do I need?
faq.a: The TOSHIBA at 1.2 cu ft suits most households of one to four people. Move up to the Sharp SMC2266KS at 2.2 cu ft for large dishes, or drop to the COMFEE' at 0.7 cu ft for a dorm.

Buying by capacity alone. A 1.6 cu ft unit with no listed wattage, like the Panasonic NN-SN76LS, is harder to judge than the Farberware, which states 1100 watts, since power sets how long every dish takes.

faq.q: Is the Sharp worth it over the TOSHIBA?
faq.a: Only if you need a 2.2 cu ft interior and 1200W for big dishes. Otherwise the TOSHIBA's 1000W is enough, and it costs less, takes less counter and heats just as quickly for most meals.

faq.q: How do I use sensor cooking?
faq.a: Pick the matching auto cook setting and let the microwave sense steam. The Farberware lists Smart Sensor Auto Cook, so use that mode for plates of leftovers instead of guessing a time and stopping to stir.

faq.q: How do I keep it clean?
faq.a: Wipe the interior after spills with a damp cloth and avoid harsh scrubbing on the walls. Check the manual for turntable care, and clean the door seal edges regularly so food residue does not build up and hold the door slightly open.
Yes. The COMFEE' at 700W needs more time than the Panasonic NN-SN686S at 1200W for the same plate, and the gap is larger on dense or frozen food, so budget extra minutes on the smaller unit.

finalTake: Buy the TOSHIBA unless something specific points elsewhere. Choose the Sharp for big dishes and a large family, the Panasonic NN-SN686S if speed matters and the budget allows, and the Farberware for sensor reheating. The COMFEE' fits a dorm or office, and the NN-SN76LS suits buyers who verify the footprint and accept the missing wattage.
